name: Watterson Estimator Calculator
seoDesc: The Watterson estimator infers the population mutation parameter θ from the number of segregating sites in a sample, with a correction for how many sequences
summary:
The Watterson estimator infers the population mutation parameter θ from the number of segregating sites in a sample, with a correction for how many sequences you sequenced. It returns harmonic number a₁ (n − 1), watterson θ (per locus), θ per site and watterson θ per kb, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is the quickest way to compare diversity between samples of different sizes and to spot a population that is not at equilibrium. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Watterson Estimator
sections.html:
θ_W = S ÷ a₁, where a₁ = Σ 1/i for i = 1 … n−1

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Snumber of segregating sitessites
nnumber of sequences in the samplesequences
a₁harmonic number of n − 1—

sections.title: How do I use the Watterson Estimator?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: segregating sites of 24, sequence length of 1,000 bp, number of sequences of 20.

Substituting them into the formula gives harmonic number a₁ (n − 1) of 3.55, watterson θ (per locus) of 6.76, θ per site of 0.0068, watterson θ per kb of 6.76.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0 – 0.001Low diversitybottleneck, inbreeding or a small population
0.001 – 0.01Typicalmany outcrossing eukaryotes
0.01 – 0.05Highlarge populations, viruses, bacteria
above 0.05Very highoften a sign of recent admixture

  • θ_W uses only the count of variable sites, so it is cheap to compute and stable, but it is sensitive to sample size through a₁.

  • Comparing θ_W with π (average pairwise difference) is the basis of Tajima's D: they agree under a standard neutral model and diverge under selection or demographic change.

  • The estimator assumes an infinite-sites model with no recombination within the locus. Recombining data must be split into blocks.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Forgetting the a₁ correction and dividing S by n.
  • Comparing θ from samples of very different sizes without noting a₁.
  • Applying it to a locus with recombination, which biases θ downward.

faq.q: Why is a₁ in the denominator?
faq.a: Because the expected number of segregating sites grows with the harmonic number of the sample size under the neutral coalescent.

faq.q: Can θ_W estimate effective population size?
faq.a: Yes, for a neutral locus: θ = 4Nₑμ for a diploid autosome, so Nₑ = θ ÷ (4μ).

faq.q: What does the Watterson Estimator actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns harmonic number a₁ (n − 1), watterson θ (per locus), θ per site and watterson θ per kb. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
